content.overview: A perpetual injunction prevents breach of an obligation in the plaintiff's favour, including property rights as enacted.
content.study: Temporary injunctions are CPC Order XXXIX. Final injunctions are SRA 38 and 39. Mandatory injunction is 39. An injunction that amounts to specific performance of a 14 contract will fail.

learningObjectives: Explain when a perpetual injunction may be granted under Section 38.
Distinguish perpetual injunctions from temporary and mandatory injunctions.
Apply the statutory property-invasion grounds and the contract cross-reference.
enhancement.definition: Section 38 permits a perpetual injunction to prevent breach of an obligation and, where property rights are invaded or threatened, identifies specified circumstances in which perpetual injunctive relief may be granted.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Perpetual injunction is final preventive relief granted by decree. For property-right invasions, Section 38(3) identifies statutory circumstances including absence of a reliable damages standard, inadequacy of monetary compensation, trustee relationships and prevention of multiplicity of proceedings.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Specific Relief Act, 1963, Sections 36–38, particularly Section 38(1)–(3); temporary injunctions are regulated by CPC, while mandatory injunctions are addressed separately in Section 39.
essentialIngredients: Identify an obligation existing in the plaintiff's favour.
For contractual obligations, apply the Chapter II rules where relevant.
If property rights are invaded or threatened, test the Section 38(3) grounds.
Distinguish the final perpetual relief from temporary relief under CPC Order XXXIX.
Ensure the relief sought is legally compatible with the restrictions in the injunction chapter.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 38 governs final preventive relief. A perpetual injunction is granted by decree after adjudication on the merits. The section operates both for obligations generally and for specified property-right invasions. In property cases, the court examines the statutory grounds and the adequacy of damages. The remedy should be matched to the right being protected; where a plaintiff also needs possession or another consequential remedy, the pleading should address that relief rather than relying on an injunction alone.
examples: If a defendant threatens repeated interference with a plaintiff's established property right and monetary compensation would not adequately protect the right, the plaintiff may frame a claim for perpetual injunction under the statutory grounds, subject to the other requirements of the Act.
enhancement.distinctions: Section 38 concerns perpetual injunctions; Section 37 distinguishes temporary and perpetual injunctions; Section 39 concerns mandatory injunctions; Section 41 specifies situations where injunctions are refused.

caseLaw.name: Samar Kumar Roy v. Jharna Bera
caseLaw.citation: Civil Appeal No. 11200 of 2017; Supreme Court, 5 Sep 2017
caseLaw.holding: The Supreme Court considered declaratory and perpetual-injunction relief under Sections 34 and 38 in the context of the pleaded rights and reliefs.
caseLaw.relevance: Illustrates the combined operation of declaratory and perpetual-injunction claims.

enhancement.problemApplication: A plaintiff alleges repeated interference with a property right. Identify the underlying right, the obligation breached or threatened, the applicable Section 38(3) ground, and whether another consequential remedy must also be sought.
examAnswerStructure: Identify the protected right or obligation.
State Section 38 and the relevant ground.
Apply the facts to the statutory conditions.
Consider related consequential relief and Section 41 restrictions.
Conclude on the availability of a perpetual injunction.
keyTakeaways: Perpetual injunction is final relief granted by decree after adjudication on the merits.
Section 38(3) contains specific property-invasion grounds; adequacy of damages is central in several of them.
Always distinguish Section 38 from temporary injunctions under CPC and mandatory injunctions under Section 39.
